course.title: Biochemistry
course.description: The chemistry of life — how water, amino acids, sugars, lipids, and nucleic acids assemble into living systems, and how metabolism captures and spends energy through pathways like glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation. Structure adapted from OpenStax Biology and Chemistry (CC BY 4.0); all explanations original.

questions.prompt: The property of water most responsible for dissolving salts and polar molecules is that water is…
questions.explanation: Water's bent shape gives oxygen a partial negative and each hydrogen a partial positive charge, so it surrounds and separates ions — see 'Water, pH, and buffers'.

questions.prompt: A solution with pH = 3 compared to one with pH = 6 has a hydrogen ion concentration that is…
questions.explanation: pH is a base-10 log scale, so a drop of 3 pH units means 10^3 = 1000 times more H+.

questions.prompt: The monomers that link by peptide bonds to build proteins are…
questions.explanation: Amino acids join head-to-tail through peptide bonds — see 'Amino acids and protein structure'.

questions.prompt: An enzyme speeds a reaction primarily by…
questions.explanation: Catalysts lower the activation-energy barrier; they do not change where equilibrium sits.

questions.prompt: The base that pairs with adenine in DNA is…
questions.explanation: In DNA, A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and G pairs with C — see 'Nucleic acids'.

questions.prompt: The cell's main short-term energy currency is…
questions.explanation: ATP stores readily released energy in its phosphate bonds and is spent across the cell.

questions.prompt: Glycolysis converts one glucose molecule into two molecules of…
questions.explanation: Glycolysis ends at two three-carbon pyruvate molecules — see 'Glycolysis and the citric acid cycle'.

questions.prompt: Most ATP in aerobic cells is produced during…
questions.explanation: The electron transport chain plus ATP synthase make the large majority of ATP — see 'Oxidative phosphorylation'.

lessons.title: Water, pH, and buffers
lessons.grammar_note: pH is a logarithm: each whole pH unit is a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration, so pH 5 is ten times more acidic than pH 6.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why water is the solvent of life, compute pH from hydrogen ion concentration, and use the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation to predict how a buffer resists pH change. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, how many times more acidic is a pH 3 solution than a pH 6 one?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Water is a polar molecule: oxygen pulls electron density away from its two hydrogens, leaving oxygen partially negative and the hydrogens partially positive. These partial charges let water form hydrogen bonds and dissolve ions and other polar molecules, while nonpolar molecules cluster away from water (the hydrophobic effect that drives membranes to form). Water also self-ionizes slightly: H2O -> H+ + OH-, with the product [H+][OH-] = 1e-14 at 25 C. We measure acidity as pH = -log[H+]. Pure water has [H+] = 1e-7, so pH = 7 (neutral); lower pH is acidic, higher pH is basic. A buffer is a mixture of a weak acid HA and its conjugate base A- that soaks up added H+ or OH- with only a small pH shift. Its behavior follows pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, where pKa is the pH at which the acid is half dissociated. A buffer works best when pH is near its pKa, because then the ratio [A-]/[HA] is close to 1 and can move in either direction.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Compute pH of a solution with [H+] = 1e-4: pH = -log(1e-4) = 4, acidic. Equal parts acid and base: for acetic acid (pKa = 4.76) with [A-] = [HA], log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa + 0 = 4.76. Blood's bicarbonate buffer: pKa = 6.1, with [HCO3-] = 24 mM and dissolved CO2 = 1.2 mM, the ratio is 24 / 1.2 = 20, and log(20) = 1.3, so pH = 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4 — exactly physiological pH. Reverse it: to hold pH = pKa + 1, you need log([A-]/[HA]) = 1, i.e. a 10:1 ratio of base to acid.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the pH when [H+] = 1e-2? 2) A buffer has pKa = 7.2; if [A-]/[HA] = 1, what is its pH? 3) Using pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), find pH when pKa = 4.76 and [A-]/[HA] = 10. 4) Which buffer better controls pH near 7.4: one with pKa 4.8 or one with pKa 7.2? 5) If [H+] = 1e-9, is the solution acidic or basic? Answers: 1) -log(1e-2) = 2. 2) log(1) = 0, so pH = 7.2. 3) 4.76 + log(10) = 4.76 + 1 = 5.76. 4) pKa 7.2, because a buffer is strongest within about one unit of its pKa. 5) pH = 9, which is basic (above 7).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating pH as linear — going from pH 7 to pH 4 is a 1000-fold, not a threefold, change in [H+]. Mistake: expecting a buffer to work far from its pKa; outside roughly pKa plus or minus 1, one form runs out and the pH swings. Exit: (a) Write the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation. (b) At what ratio of [A-] to [HA] does pH equal pKa? Answers: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]); a 1:1 ratio, since log(1) = 0.

lessons.title: Amino acids and protein structure
lessons.grammar_note: Proteins are read and built from the amino (N) end to the carboxyl (C) end; sequence is always written N-terminus first.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the parts of an amino acid, describe how the side chain sets its chemistry, and distinguish the four levels of protein structure. Warm-up: what kind of bond joins two amino acids together?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Every amino acid has a central carbon bonded to an amino group (-NH2), a carboxyl group (-COOH), a hydrogen, and a variable side chain (R group). The 20 standard side chains fall into groups: nonpolar and hydrophobic, polar uncharged, acidic (negative), and basic (positive). A peptide bond forms when the carboxyl of one amino acid condenses with the amino group of the next, releasing water. Protein structure has four levels. Primary structure is the amino acid sequence. Secondary structure is local folding into alpha helices and beta sheets, held by backbone hydrogen bonds. Tertiary structure is the full three-dimensional fold of one chain, driven largely by the hydrophobic effect (nonpolar side chains bury inward, away from water) plus hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, and disulfide bridges. Quaternary structure is the assembly of two or more folded chains into one complex, as in hemoglobin's four subunits.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Building a tripeptide from three amino acids uses two peptide bonds and releases two water molecules. Predicting placement: a leucine (nonpolar) side chain tends to sit in the buried core, while a glutamate (acidic, charged) side chain tends to sit on the water-facing surface. Reading direction: the sequence Gly-Ala-Ser starts at the free amino group of glycine (the N-terminus) and ends at the free carboxyl of serine (the C-terminus). Denaturation: heating or extreme pH breaks the weak interactions holding tertiary structure, so the chain unfolds and loses function even though every peptide bond stays intact — sequence survives, shape does not.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the four groups bonded to the central carbon of an amino acid. 2) How many peptide bonds are in a chain of 50 amino acids? 3) Which structural level is the amino acid sequence itself? 4) Would a valine (nonpolar) side chain more likely face water or the buried core? 5) What holds alpha helices and beta sheets together? Answers: 1) amino group, carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and the R side chain. 2) 49 — one fewer than the number of residues. 3) primary structure. 4) the buried core, away from water. 5) hydrogen bonds along the polypeptide backbone.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing secondary and tertiary structure — secondary is local backbone patterns (helices, sheets); tertiary is the whole chain's 3D shape. Mistake: thinking denaturation cuts the chain; it only unravels folding, leaving the primary sequence intact. Exit: (a) What bond links amino acids? (b) Which level of structure describes several chains assembling together? Answers: the peptide bond; quaternary structure.

lessons.title: Protein function and enzymes: kinetics and Michaelis-Menten
lessons.grammar_note: Km has units of concentration (it is a substrate concentration); a small Km means high affinity, because half-maximal speed is reached at a low substrate level.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how enzymes catalyze reactions, read a Michaelis-Menten curve, and use v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]) to compute reaction rates. Warm-up: does a catalyst change how much product is possible at equilibrium, or only how fast you get there?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An enzyme is usually a protein whose folded shape creates an active site that binds a substrate and lowers the activation energy of its reaction, speeding it up without being consumed. Enzymes do not change the equilibrium or the overall free-energy change; they change the rate. Most enzymes follow Michaelis-Menten kinetics: rate v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]), where Vmax is the maximum rate when the enzyme is saturated and Km is the substrate concentration that gives exactly half of Vmax. A low Km means the enzyme reaches half speed at low substrate — high affinity; a high Km means it needs a lot of substrate — low affinity. The turnover number kcat is how many substrate molecules one active site converts per second at saturation, and kcat/Km measures overall catalytic efficiency. Inhibitors slow enzymes: a competitive inhibitor competes for the active site and raises the apparent Km, while a noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and lowers Vmax.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Half-speed check: set [S] = Km in v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]). Then v = Vmax·Km / (Km + Km) = Vmax·Km / (2Km) = Vmax/2 — this is why Km is the half-maximal substrate concentration. Numeric rate: with Vmax = 100 micromol/min and Km = 2 mM, at [S] = 6 mM, v = 100·6 / (2 + 6) = 600 / 8 = 75 micromol/min. At very high [S] = 200 mM, v = 100·200 / (2 + 200) = 20000 / 202 = 99, nearly Vmax — the enzyme is almost saturated. Affinity comparison: enzyme X with Km = 0.1 mM binds substrate more tightly than enzyme Y with Km = 5 mM, because X hits half speed at a fiftyfold lower substrate level.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]), what is v when [S] = Km? 2) With Vmax = 80 and Km = 4 mM, find v at [S] = 4 mM. 3) With Vmax = 80 and Km = 4 mM, find v at [S] = 12 mM. 4) Which enzyme has higher substrate affinity: Km = 0.5 mM or Km = 10 mM? 5) Does a catalyst change the equilibrium position of a reaction? Answers: 1) v = Vmax/2. 2) at [S] = Km, v = 80/2 = 40. 3) 80·12 / (4 + 12) = 960 / 16 = 60. 4) Km = 0.5 mM (lower Km, higher affinity). 5) No — it only speeds the approach to the same equilibrium.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading a high Km as strong binding — it is the opposite; high Km means weak affinity. Mistake: claiming an enzyme shifts equilibrium or gets used up; it does neither. Exit: (a) At what rate does an enzyme run when [S] equals Km? (b) A competitive inhibitor changes which parameter's apparent value? Answers: half of Vmax; it raises the apparent Km.

questions.prompt: A solution has [H+] = 1e-5. Its pH is…
Using pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), a buffer with pKa = 6.1 and a 20:1 ratio of base to acid has pH…
The hydrophobic effect drives protein folding by pushing which side chains toward the buried core?
questions.explanation: Nonpolar side chains cluster away from water in the interior of the fold.

questions.prompt: A chain of 100 amino acids contains how many peptide bonds?
questions.explanation: There is one peptide bond between each adjacent pair, so 99.

questions.prompt: In v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]) with Vmax = 60 and Km = 3 mM, the rate at [S] = 3 mM is…
questions.explanation: At [S] = Km the rate is half of Vmax, so 30.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme binds its substrate more tightly?
questions.explanation: A lower Km means half-maximal speed at lower substrate, so higher affinity.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates
lessons.grammar_note: The suffix -ose marks a sugar (glucose, fructose, lactose); mono-, di-, and poly- count how many sugar units are linked.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Classify carbohydrates by size, explain glycosidic bonds, and contrast storage and structural polysaccharides. Warm-up: what two smaller sugars combine to make sucrose, ordinary table sugar?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Carbohydrates are built from monosaccharides — simple sugars such as glucose and fructose, most with the general formula (CH2O)n. Two monosaccharides join by a glycosidic bond, formed by condensation (losing water), to make a disaccharide: glucose + fructose gives sucrose, and glucose + galactose gives lactose. Many units linked together form a polysaccharide. The same glucose monomer builds very different polymers depending on the bond geometry: starch and glycogen use alpha linkages that coil and are easy to digest for energy storage (glycogen is the animal form, branched for fast mobilization), while cellulose uses beta linkages that form straight, tough fibers for plant cell walls that most animals cannot digest. So the bond type, not just the monomer, determines whether a polysaccharide is fuel or structure.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Naming by size: glucose is a monosaccharide (one unit), maltose is a disaccharide (two glucose units), and glycogen is a polysaccharide (thousands of glucose units). Counting water: linking 5 glucose units into a chain forms 4 glycosidic bonds and releases 4 water molecules, one per bond. Storage versus structure: starch and cellulose are both glucose polymers, yet you can digest starch for energy and not cellulose, because the alpha versus beta linkage changes the shape and which enzymes can cut it. Breaking down: digestion is hydrolysis — adding water across each glycosidic bond splits a disaccharide back into two monosaccharides.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) How many monosaccharide units are in a disaccharide? 2) What monosaccharides make up sucrose? 3) How many glycosidic bonds link a chain of 10 glucose units? 4) Which glucose polymer is used for structure in plants? 5) Is forming a glycosidic bond a condensation (water released) or hydrolysis (water added)? Answers: 1) two. 2) glucose and fructose. 3) 9 — one fewer than the number of units. 4) cellulose. 5) condensation, which releases one water per bond.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming the same monomer must give the same material — starch and cellulose share glucose but differ entirely because of alpha versus beta linkages. Mistake: mixing up condensation (bond forms, water leaves) with hydrolysis (bond breaks, water enters). Exit: (a) What bond joins two sugars? (b) Which is the animal energy-storage polysaccharide, glycogen or cellulose? Answers: a glycosidic bond; glycogen.

lessons.title: Lipids and membranes
lessons.grammar_note: Amphipathic means one molecule has both a water-loving (hydrophilic) part and a water-fearing (hydrophobic) part — the key to why membranes form.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the main lipid classes, explain why phospholipids spontaneously form bilayers, and connect membrane structure to its function. Warm-up: why does oil refuse to mix into water?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Lipids are a diverse group united by being largely nonpolar and insoluble in water. Fatty acids are long hydrocarbon chains ending in a carboxyl group; they are saturated (no carbon-carbon double bonds, straight, solid-tending) or unsaturated (one or more double bonds that kink the chain, keeping it fluid). Triglycerides, three fatty acids on a glycerol backbone, are compact energy storage. Phospholipids replace one fatty acid with a phosphate-containing head group, making them amphipathic: a hydrophilic (polar) head and two hydrophobic (nonpolar) tails. In water, phospholipids self-assemble so tails hide from water and heads face it, forming a bilayer — the basis of every cell membrane. This bilayer is a selectively permeable, fluid mosaic: small nonpolar molecules cross easily, while ions and large polar molecules need transport proteins. Cholesterol wedges among the tails to tune fluidity. The membrane thus separates inside from outside and controls what passes.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Predicting state: a fat rich in saturated fatty acids (straight chains that pack tightly) tends to be solid at room temperature, like butter, while one rich in unsaturated fatty acids (kinked chains) tends to be liquid, like olive oil. Self-assembly: drop amphipathic phospholipids into water and they spontaneously form a bilayer, because burying the tails and exposing the heads lowers the system's free energy — no energy input required. Permeability: oxygen (small, nonpolar) diffuses straight through the bilayer, but a sodium ion (charged) cannot and must move through a channel or pump. Storage math: a triglyceride carries three fatty acids per glycerol, packing more energy per gram than carbohydrate because its carbons are highly reduced.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does amphipathic mean? 2) Which part of a phospholipid faces the watery inside and outside of a cell? 3) Saturated or unsaturated fats are more likely solid at room temperature? 4) Can a charged ion cross a bilayer freely? 5) How many fatty acids are in one triglyceride? Answers: 1) having both a water-loving and a water-fearing region. 2) the hydrophilic phosphate head groups. 3) saturated, because straight chains pack tightly. 4) no — it needs a transport protein or channel. 5) three, attached to one glycerol.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking membranes must be built by an energy-driven process — bilayers self-assemble because it is thermodynamically favorable. Mistake: assuming everything crosses the membrane equally; the bilayer is selectively permeable. Exit: (a) What structure do phospholipids form in water? (b) Which type of fatty acid, saturated or unsaturated, kinks the chain? Answers: a bilayer; unsaturated (its double bonds create the kink).

lessons.title: Nucleic acids: DNA and RNA structure
lessons.grammar_note: DNA uses the base thymine (T); RNA swaps in uracil (U) instead. Both still pair with adenine (A).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Identify the parts of a nucleotide, apply base-pairing rules, and contrast DNA with RNA. Warm-up: in DNA, which base pairs with cytosine?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three parts: a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base. The bases are purines (adenine A, guanine G) and pyrimidines (cytosine C, thymine T in DNA, uracil U in RNA). Nucleotides link through their sugar and phosphate into a backbone with directionality, running 5-prime to 3-prime. DNA is double-stranded: two backbones wind into a double helix, and the strands are complementary and antiparallel, held by base pairs — A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and G pairs with C (three hydrogen bonds). Because G-C pairs share an extra hydrogen bond, GC-rich DNA is more stable and harder to separate. RNA differs in three ways: its sugar is ribose (not deoxyribose), it uses uracil in place of thymine, and it is usually single-stranded, letting it fold into shapes that do jobs such as carrying messages (mRNA), forming ribosomes (rRNA), and delivering amino acids (tRNA).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Base-pairing: the DNA strand 5-ATGC-3 pairs with the complementary antiparallel strand 3-TACG-5. Chargaff check: if a genome is 30 percent A, then it is 30 percent T (A pairs with T), leaving 40 percent split evenly as 20 percent G and 20 percent C. Stability: a stretch that is mostly G-C melts at a higher temperature than one that is mostly A-T, because each G-C pair adds a third hydrogen bond. RNA transcription pairing: a DNA template 3-TACG-5 is read into the RNA 5-AUGC-3 — note uracil appears where DNA would have used thymine.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three parts of a nucleotide. 2) In DNA, which base pairs with guanine? 3) If a DNA sample is 20 percent cytosine, what percent is guanine? 4) Give the RNA sequence complementary to the DNA template 3-TAC-5. 5) Which base replaces thymine in RNA? Answers: 1) a sugar, a phosphate, and a nitrogenous base. 2) cytosine (G-C, three hydrogen bonds). 3) 20 percent — C pairs with G in equal amounts. 4) 5-AUG-3 (uracil pairs with the template adenine). 5) uracil.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forgetting the strands are antiparallel — one runs 5-to-3 while its partner runs 3-to-5. Mistake: writing thymine into RNA; RNA uses uracil. Exit: (a) How many hydrogen bonds hold a G-C pair? (b) Which sugar is in RNA? Answers: three; ribose.

lessons.title: The central dogma: replication, transcription, translation
lessons.grammar_note: The genetic code is read in triplets called codons; 3 mRNA bases specify 1 amino acid, and there are 4^3 = 64 possible codons.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Trace how genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein, and read a codon into its amino acid. Warm-up: how many DNA or RNA letters code for a single amino acid?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The central dogma describes the flow of genetic information: DNA is copied (replication), transcribed into RNA (transcription), and RNA is decoded into protein (translation). Replication is semiconservative — the double helix unzips and each old strand templates a new complementary strand, so each daughter molecule keeps one original strand. Transcription copies one gene's template strand into a messenger RNA (mRNA), using the same base-pairing rules but writing uracil for thymine. Translation happens on the ribosome, which reads the mRNA three bases at a time. Each three-base codon specifies one amino acid; there are 4^3 = 64 codons for 20 amino acids, so the code is redundant (several codons can mean the same amino acid). Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) match their anticodons to codons and bring the matching amino acids, which the ribosome joins by peptide bonds. A start codon (AUG) begins the protein and stop codons end it. This is biochemistry in action: base-pairing and enzyme catalysis turn a stored sequence into a working molecule.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Transcription: the DNA template strand 3-TAC-GGA-5 is transcribed into mRNA 5-AUG-CCU-3, swapping U for T. Codon count: an mRNA of 30 coding bases carries 30 / 3 = 10 codons, so up to 10 amino acids (minus one for the stop codon). Redundancy: because 64 codons encode only 20 amino acids plus stop signals, many amino acids have more than one codon — a change in the third base often encodes the same amino acid. Semiconservative proof: after one round of replication, every daughter double helix is one old strand paired with one brand-new strand, which is exactly what the classic density experiment observed.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) List the three processes of the central dogma in order. 2) What does semiconservative replication mean? 3) How many bases make one codon? 4) How many codons are possible in total? 5) Transcribe the DNA template 3-TACGGG-5 into mRNA. Answers: 1) replication, transcription, translation. 2) each new double helix keeps one original strand and one new strand. 3) three. 4) 4^3 = 64. 5) 5-AUGCCC-3 (U replaces T; each base pairs with its template partner).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking replication makes two all-new helices — it is semiconservative, keeping one parental strand each. Mistake: reading mRNA one base at a time; the ribosome reads triplets. Exit: (a) How many bases specify one amino acid? (b) Which molecule carries amino acids to the ribosome? Answers: three (a codon); transfer RNA (tRNA).

questions.prompt: Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose but behave differently because of…
questions.explanation: The linkage geometry (alpha versus beta) changes shape and digestibility.

questions.prompt: Phospholipids form a bilayer in water because they are…
questions.explanation: Amphipathic molecules bury their tails and expose their heads, forming a bilayer.

questions.prompt: If a DNA sample is 30 percent adenine, what percent is guanine?
questions.explanation: A = T = 30 percent leaves 40 percent for G+C, split evenly as 20 percent each.

questions.prompt: A G-C base pair is held by how many hydrogen bonds?
questions.explanation: G-C pairs share three hydrogen bonds, making them more stable than A-T pairs.

questions.prompt: How many codons are possible from a four-letter genetic alphabet read in triplets?
questions.explanation: 4^3 = 64 possible codons.

questions.prompt: DNA replication is described as semiconservative because each new double helix contains…
options: one old and one new strand
questions.explanation: Each daughter helix keeps one parental strand paired with a new one.

lessons.title: Metabolism overview and bioenergetics: ATP and free energy
lessons.grammar_note: A negative free-energy change (delta G less than 0) marks a spontaneous, energy-releasing reaction; a positive delta G reaction must be driven by coupling it to one that releases more.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish catabolism from anabolism, read the sign of free-energy change, and explain how ATP couples energy-releasing to energy-requiring reactions. Warm-up: which stores more usable energy, ATP or its product ADP?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Metabolism is the whole set of chemical reactions in a cell, split into catabolism (breaking molecules down to release energy) and anabolism (building molecules using energy). The direction a reaction runs is set by the Gibbs free-energy change, delta G. When delta G is negative the reaction is exergonic (spontaneous, releasing energy); when positive it is endergonic (requires an input). The full expression is delta G = delta G-standard + RT ln(Q), where Q compares actual product and reactant amounts to standard conditions — so cells can push reactions by keeping products low or reactants high. ATP is the cell's energy currency: hydrolyzing ATP to ADP plus phosphate is strongly exergonic, with a standard delta G of about -30.5 kJ/mol (about -7.3 kcal/mol). Cells couple this favorable release to unfavorable reactions, so the pair together has a negative delta G and proceeds. Electron carriers NADH and FADH2 hold energy in a second form — high-energy electrons — that oxidative phosphorylation later converts into ATP.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Reading signs: a reaction with delta G = -20 kJ/mol runs forward on its own; one with delta G = +15 kJ/mol does not, unless coupled. Coupling arithmetic: making glutamine from glutamate costs about +14 kJ/mol; couple it to ATP hydrolysis at about -30.5 kJ/mol and the sum is 14 + (-30.5) = -16.5 kJ/mol, now spontaneous. Direction from concentrations: even a reaction with a small positive delta G-standard can run forward if products are continually removed, because the RT ln(Q) term becomes negative when Q is small. Currency logic: cells keep the ATP-to-ADP ratio high, so ATP hydrolysis stays far from equilibrium and delivers usable energy on demand.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Is a reaction with delta G = -12 kJ/mol exergonic or endergonic? 2) Which process releases energy, catabolism or anabolism? 3) A reaction needs +10 kJ/mol; coupled to ATP hydrolysis (-30.5 kJ/mol), what is the combined delta G? 4) Does hydrolyzing ATP to ADP release or absorb energy? 5) In delta G = delta G-standard + RT ln(Q), what happens to delta G when products are kept very low (small Q)? Answers: 1) exergonic (negative delta G). 2) catabolism. 3) 10 + (-30.5) = -20.5 kJ/mol, spontaneous. 4) it releases energy (strongly exergonic). 5) the ln(Q) term becomes negative, lowering delta G and favoring the forward reaction.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming a positive-delta-G reaction can never happen — coupling to ATP or shifting concentrations can drive it. Mistake: thinking ATP stores energy for the long term; it is a short-term currency, constantly made and spent, while glucose and fat are the reserves. Exit: (a) What is the sign of delta G for a spontaneous reaction? (b) What molecule couples energy-releasing to energy-requiring reactions? Answers: negative; ATP.

lessons.title: Glycolysis and the citric acid cycle
lessons.grammar_note: Track the carbon count: glucose (6 carbons) splits into two pyruvate (3 carbons each), then each becomes acetyl-CoA (2 carbons) after releasing one CO2.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Summarize the inputs and outputs of glycolysis and the citric acid cycle and tally the energy carriers they yield per glucose. Warm-up: how many carbons are in one glucose molecule, and how many in one pyruvate?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and splits one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules. It first invests 2 ATP, then produces 4 ATP, for a net gain of 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH per glucose. No oxygen is needed for glycolysis itself. When oxygen is present, each pyruvate is oxidized to a two-carbon acetyl group attached to coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA), releasing one CO2 and making 1 NADH — so two per glucose. Acetyl-CoA enters the citric acid cycle (also called the Krebs or TCA cycle) in the mitochondrion. Each turn of the cycle fully oxidizes the acetyl group to 2 CO2 and captures energy as 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 ATP (as GTP). Because each glucose gives two acetyl-CoA, the cycle turns twice per glucose. The point of these stages is less about direct ATP and more about loading up the electron carriers NADH and FADH2, which feed the next stage.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Net glycolysis ATP: 4 produced minus 2 invested = 2 net ATP per glucose, plus 2 NADH. Doubling for the cycle: since one glucose yields two pyruvate and thus two acetyl-CoA, everything after glycolysis counts twice — the citric acid cycle's per-turn 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP becomes 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 2 GTP per glucose. Full carrier tally per glucose so far: glycolysis 2 NADH; pyruvate to acetyl-CoA 2 NADH; citric acid cycle 6 NADH and 2 FADH2 — a total of 10 NADH and 2 FADH2, plus 4 ATP/GTP made directly (2 from glycolysis, 2 from the cycle). Carbon bookkeeping: the 6 carbons of glucose all leave as CO2 — 2 in forming the two acetyl-CoA and 4 across the two cycle turns.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the net ATP yield of glycolysis per glucose? 2) How many pyruvate come from one glucose? 3) How many times does the citric acid cycle turn per glucose? 4) Per glucose, how many NADH come from the citric acid cycle alone? 5) Counting all stages through the cycle, how many NADH does one glucose yield? Answers: 1) 2 net ATP. 2) two. 3) twice, one per acetyl-CoA. 4) 6 (3 per turn, two turns). 5) 10 (2 from glycolysis, 2 from pyruvate oxidation, 6 from the cycle).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reporting glycolysis as 4 ATP — the gross is 4, but net is 2 after the 2-ATP investment. Mistake: forgetting to double the citric acid cycle's output per glucose; it runs twice. Exit: (a) What three-carbon molecule ends glycolysis? (b) How many NADH plus FADH2 does one full glucose oxidation load, counting all stages before oxidative phosphorylation? Answers: pyruvate; 10 NADH and 2 FADH2.

lessons.title: Oxidative phosphorylation
lessons.grammar_note: Chemiosmosis: energy is stored as a proton (H+) gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane, then released as protons flow back through ATP synthase to make ATP.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how the electron transport chain and ATP synthase turn NADH and FADH2 into ATP, and estimate the total ATP yield per glucose. Warm-up: what is the final electron acceptor that makes this stage aerobic?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Oxidative phosphorylation is where the electron carriers loaded earlier pay off. NADH and FADH2 drop their high-energy electrons into the electron transport chain, a series of protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane. As electrons pass down the chain to progressively more electron-hungry acceptors, the complexes pump protons (H+) from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building an electrochemical gradient. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor: it collects the spent electrons and combines with protons to form water, which is why the process needs oxygen and is called aerobic. The stored proton gradient then drives ATP synthase, a molecular turbine: protons flow back into the matrix through it, and that flow powers the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP — a mechanism called chemiosmosis. Using common estimates of about 2.5 ATP per NADH and about 1.5 ATP per FADH2, a single glucose yields roughly 30 to 32 ATP in total across all stages.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Per-carrier estimate: 10 NADH at about 2.5 ATP each gives about 25 ATP; 2 FADH2 at about 1.5 ATP each gives about 3 ATP; that is about 28 ATP from oxidative phosphorylation. Grand total: add the 4 ATP/GTP made directly in glycolysis and the citric acid cycle, and one glucose yields about 28 + 4 = 32 ATP (commonly quoted as 30 to 32, since shuttling glycolytic NADH into the mitochondrion can cost a little). Why FADH2 gives less: it enters the chain later than NADH, so its electrons pump fewer protons, yielding less ATP. Oxygen's role: block the final acceptor and the whole chain backs up, proton pumping stops, and ATP output collapses even though earlier stages could still run briefly.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration? 2) What gradient does the electron transport chain build? 3) Which enzyme uses the proton gradient to make ATP? 4) Using 2.5 ATP per NADH, how much ATP comes from 10 NADH? 5) About how many total ATP does one glucose yield? Answers: 1) oxygen (forming water). 2) a proton (H+) gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane. 3) ATP synthase. 4) 10 x 2.5 = 25 ATP. 5) roughly 30 to 32 ATP.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the electron transport chain makes ATP directly — it pumps protons; ATP synthase makes the ATP from the resulting gradient. Mistake: forgetting oxygen's role, without which the chain halts. Exit: (a) What process couples the proton gradient to ATP synthesis? (b) Roughly how much ATP does full aerobic oxidation of one glucose give? Answers: chemiosmosis (through ATP synthase); about 30 to 32 ATP.

questions.prompt: A reaction with delta G = -25 kJ/mol is…
questions.explanation: A negative delta G means the reaction releases energy and proceeds spontaneously.

questions.prompt: The net ATP yield of glycolysis per glucose is…
questions.explanation: Gross 4 ATP minus the 2 ATP invested gives a net of 2.

questions.prompt: Counting all stages before oxidative phosphorylation, one glucose loads how many NADH?
questions.explanation: 2 (glycolysis) + 2 (pyruvate oxidation) + 6 (citric acid cycle) = 10 NADH.

questions.prompt: In oxidative phosphorylation, ATP synthase is powered by…
options: a proton gradient flowing back across the membrane
questions.explanation: Protons flowing back through ATP synthase drive ATP synthesis — chemiosmosis.

questions.prompt: The final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration is…
questions.explanation: Oxygen accepts the spent electrons and forms water, making the process aerobic.

questions.prompt: Using about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2, the roughly estimated total ATP per glucose is…
questions.explanation: About 25 from NADH, 3 from FADH2, plus 4 direct, near 30 to 32 total.

lessons.title: Capstone: tracing energy and information through the cell
lessons.grammar_note: The molecules of life and their pathways interlock — the same free-energy and base-pairing rules govern a buffer, an enzyme, and the electron transport chain alike.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Connect the whole course: follow a glucose molecule from digestion to ATP, and follow genetic information from DNA to a working enzyme, seeing how every stage reuses the same chemistry. Warm-up: which single molecule links glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation as the shared energy currency?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Biochemistry is one connected system. Water's polarity and pH set the stage — enzymes only fold and work within a buffered pH range, which is why the bicarbonate buffer holding blood near pH 7.4 matters. Proteins, built from amino acids and folded by the hydrophobic effect, become the enzymes that catalyze nearly every reaction, obeying Michaelis-Menten kinetics. Carbohydrates and lipids are the fuel and the membranes: glucose feeds catabolism, while the phospholipid bilayer both encloses the cell and, at the mitochondrion, provides the very membrane across which oxidative phosphorylation pumps protons. Nucleic acids store and transmit the instructions: DNA is replicated, transcribed to RNA, and translated into those same proteins, closing the loop. Energy flows through all of it as ATP, minted wherever a negative delta G reaction can be coupled to phosphorylating ADP. Understanding one pathway means understanding how it hands off to the next.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Fuel path, end to end: a starch molecule is hydrolyzed to glucose; glycolysis nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH and makes 2 pyruvate; pyruvate oxidation and two turns of the citric acid cycle release the carbons as CO2 and load 10 NADH and 2 FADH2 total; oxidative phosphorylation converts those carriers into the bulk of about 30 to 32 ATP per glucose, using oxygen as the final electron acceptor. Information path, end to end: a gene's DNA is transcribed into mRNA (U replacing T), the ribosome reads it in codons, tRNAs deliver amino acids, and peptide bonds build a chain that folds into an enzyme — for instance one of the very enzymes catalyzing glycolysis. Cross-link: that enzyme runs only because water keeps it folded and a buffer holds pH steady, tying the first lesson to the last.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which molecule is the shared energy currency across all three catabolic stages? 2) Where does oxidative phosphorylation get the membrane it needs for its proton gradient? 3) Trace the flow of genetic information in three words. 4) Why does a stable pH matter for metabolism? 5) About how much ATP does complete oxidation of one glucose yield? Answers: 1) ATP. 2) the inner mitochondrial membrane, a phospholipid bilayer. 3) DNA -> RNA -> protein. 4) enzymes only keep their folded, active shape within a narrow pH range, so buffers protect their function. 5) roughly 30 to 32 ATP.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: studying pathways as isolated lists instead of a handoff chain — glycolysis feeds the citric acid cycle, which feeds oxidative phosphorylation. Mistake: forgetting that structure (water, folding, membranes) is what lets the energy and information chemistry run at all. Exit: (a) Name the three stages of glucose catabolism in order. (b) What ties the folding of an enzyme back to the very first topic of this course? Answers: glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation; water's polarity and a buffered pH keep the enzyme folded and active.

questions.prompt: Water dissolves salts and polar molecules because it is…
questions.explanation: Water's partial charges let it surround ions and hydrogen-bond with polar molecules — 'Water, pH, and buffers'.

The peptide bond forms between the carboxyl of one amino acid and the ___ of the next.
questions.explanation: The carboxyl condenses with the next residue's amino group, releasing water.

questions.explanation: Tertiary structure is the full 3D shape of one chain.

questions.explanation: A hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails drive bilayer self-assembly.

questions.explanation: A pairs with T through two hydrogen bonds; G-C uses three.

questions.prompt: How many codons are possible in the genetic code?
questions.explanation: Triplets of four bases give 4^3 = 64 codons.

questions.prompt: DNA replication keeps one original strand in each new helix, so it is called…
questions.explanation: Each daughter helix is one old strand plus one new strand.

questions.prompt: A reaction is spontaneous (exergonic) when its free-energy change delta G is…
questions.explanation: A negative delta G means energy is released and the reaction proceeds.

questions.prompt: The net ATP and NADH yield of glycolysis per glucose is…
questions.explanation: Net 2 ATP (4 made minus 2 invested) plus 2 NADH.

questions.prompt: Counting all stages before oxidative phosphorylation, one glucose yields how many NADH and FADH2?
questions.explanation: 2 + 2 + 6 = 10 NADH, and the citric acid cycle gives 2 FADH2 per glucose.

questions.prompt: In oxidative phosphorylation, ATP is made when protons flow back through ATP synthase — a process called…
questions.explanation: Chemiosmosis couples the proton gradient to ATP synthesis.

questions.prompt: The final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain is…
questions.explanation: Oxygen accepts electrons and forms water, making respiration aerobic.

questions.prompt: Using about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2 plus 4 direct, the approximate total ATP per glucose is…
questions.explanation: About 25 (NADH) + 3 (FADH2) + 4 (direct) is near 30 to 32.
